claims.text: Nitrogen plasma immersion ion implantation at approximately 700°C with controlled dose and time will form a continuous, robust nitride-rich layer on TiB2-based components.
The implanted surface layer may contain BN-like or TiN phases.
The nitrogen implantation depth can be made several microns deep.
A treatment temperature of approximately 700°C will facilitate surface nitriding.
Molten aluminum at 750°C represents typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure conditions.
A continuous nitride-enriched layer will act as a chemical and physical barrier between TiB2 and molten aluminum.
The nitride-enriched layer will markedly lower the reactivity of the underlying boride with molten aluminum.
BN-like or TiN phases have lower chemical affinity for aluminum than the untreated TiB2-based surface.
The nitrided layer will reduce surface solubility and reactivity in molten aluminum.
Blocking direct contact at the aluminum/boride interface will slow corrosion.
Plasma-generated surface treatments or coatings can improve corrosion resistance.
Nitrogen-implanted TiB2-based components will have a lower corrosion rate in molten aluminum at 750°C than untreated TiB2-based controls.
The improved corrosion resistance will be observable as reduced weight loss and less surface degradation.
Nonuniform implantation or inadequate nitride-layer thickness may reduce corrosion protection.
The precise improvement depends on optimization of implantation dose, temperature, and duration.
Long-term stability under sustained, cyclic, or prolonged molten-aluminum exposure has not been established.
The proposed test compares nitrogen-implanted specimens with untreated controls after molten-aluminum exposure at 750°C.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in weight loss and surface degradation relative to untreated controls would falsify the predicted corrosion benefit.
